prompt: Which of the following traffic signs has the greatest number of lines of symmetry?

solutions.title: Count the lines of symmetry
solutions.body:
The second and fourth signs have no line of symmetry, the first and fifth have one, and the third (a horizontal bar in a circle) has two: one horizontal and one vertical.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Joseph draws a square with side-length 10 cm. He joins the midpoints of the sides to make a smaller square, as shown in the diagram. What is the area, in $\text{cm}^2$, of the smaller square?

solutions.title: Subtract the corners
solutions.body: Four right triangles with legs 5 cm are cut off, each of area $12.5\text{ cm}^2$. The smaller square has area $100-50=50$.

solutions.title: Halve the big square
solutions.body:
The smaller square's diagonals are the sides of the big square's halves; the square joining the midpoints is exactly half the big square. $100\div2=50$.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: Millie's mother likes her to set the table with a knife on the right-hand side of the plate and a fork on the left-hand side. Starting with the arrangement in the diagram, what is the smallest number of times Millie needs to swap the positions of a knife and a fork in order to satisfy her mother?

solutions.title: Count wrong items
solutions.body:
Four items of cutlery are in the wrong place and each swap fixes at most two of them, so at least $4\div2=2$ swaps are needed. Two swaps suffice, e.g. swap the knife and fork on the third plate, and swap the misplaced fork on the first plate with the misplaced knife on the second plate.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: On the left-hand side of the room, Jia and Lottie are sleeping with their heads on the pillows and facing each other. On the right-hand side of the room, Anaya and Isla are sleeping with their heads on the pillows with their backs to each other. How many of the girls are sleeping with their right ear on their pillow?

solutions.title: Pair by pair
solutions.body:
Two girls facing each other lie on opposite sides, so exactly one has her right ear down. The same holds for two girls with their backs to each other. So $1+1=2$.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: The piece of paper shown is folded along the dotted lines to make an open box. The box is placed on the table with the top open. What is the letter on the face that is on the table?

solutions.title: Opposite faces
solutions.body:
In the net, $P$ is opposite $S$ and $R$ is opposite $T$; no face is opposite $Q$. In an open box the base has no opposite face (the top is open), so the base is $Q$.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Which of the following figures cannot be formed by gluing these two identical squares of paper together?

solutions.title: Check each option
solutions.body:
Figure A would need an equilateral triangle at the top, but the angle there is a corner of a square, $90^\circ$, so A is impossible. The others can all be formed by overlapping two squares at suitable positions or rotations.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: 2025 is a square. How many distinct primes divide exactly into 2025?

solutions.title: Factorise
solutions.body:
$2025=45^2=(3^2\cdot5)^2=3^4\cdot5^2$, so the distinct primes are 3 and 5.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Five squirrels V, W, X, Y and Z are sitting on the line shown. There are six nuts on the line, marked with crosses. At one instant, the five squirrels start running towards the nearest nut at the same speed. As soon as a squirrel reaches a nut, it picks it up and starts running towards the next nearest nut. Which squirrel will get two nuts?

solutions.title: Track the times
solutions.body:
Measure time in units of one space. After one unit V, X, Y and Z have each reached their nearest nut, and are then 3, 3, 4 and 6 spaces from the next nearest nut. W is still 2 spaces from its nearest nut and gets there before V. The only remaining nut is the one X, Y and Z are all heading for, and X is closest, so X gets two nuts.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: There are 30 students in a class. They sit in pairs so that each boy is sitting next to a girl and exactly half of the girls are sitting next to a boy. How many boys are there in the class?

solutions.title: Count by pairs
solutions.body:
Each boy sits with a girl, so if there are $x$ boys there are $x$ girls sitting next to a boy. These are half of the girls, so there are $2x$ girls. Then $x+2x=30$ and $x=10$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: The number 2581953764 is written on a strip of paper. Dilraj cuts the strip twice and gets three numbers. Then he adds these three numbers. What is the smallest possible sum he could get?

solutions.title: Keep the pieces short
solutions.body:
Ten digits split into three pieces means some piece has at least 4 digits. The best splits are 4+3+3 digits: $2581+953+764=4298$, $258+1953+764=2975$, $258+195+3764=4217$. Other splits (4+4+2 or longer pieces) give larger sums. The smallest is 2975.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: My granny bought enough cat food to last her four cats for twelve days. However, on her way home, she found two stray cats and brought them home. Each cat was given the same amount of food each day. How many days did her cat food last?

solutions.title: Cat-days
solutions.body:
The food is $4\times12=48$ cat-days. With six cats it lasts $48\div6=8$ days.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Each letter in the eight-digit integer BENJAMIN represents one of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7. Different letters represent different digits. The integer BENJAMIN is odd and divisible by 3. Which digit is represented by $N$?

solutions.title: Digit sum
solutions.body:
$N$ appears twice and every other letter once, so the digit sum is $28+N$. The number is odd, so $N$ is odd: $28+N\in\{29,31,33,35\}$ for $N=1,3,5,7$. Only 33 is divisible by 3, so $N=5$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Tim, Tom and Jim are triplets. Their brother Carl is three years younger. Which of the following could be the sum of the ages of the four brothers?

solutions.title: Write the total
solutions.body:
If the triplets are $x$ years old, the sum is $3x+(x-3)=4x-3$, which is 3 less than a multiple of 4. Adding 3 to the options gives $56,57,59,62,66$; only 56 is a multiple of 4. So the sum is 53 (triplets 14, Carl 11).

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: The perimeter of the rectangle $PQRS$ is 30 cm. A new shape is formed by placing three other rectangles so that their centres are at the points $P$, $Q$ and $S$, as shown in the diagram. The sum of the perimeters of the three added rectangles is 20 cm. What is the total perimeter of the new shape?

solutions.title: Effect of one added rectangle
solutions.body:
A rectangle of size $2x\times2y$ centred at a corner adds $(x+2y)+(2x+y)$ to the boundary and removes $x+y$, a net gain of $2x+2y$, which is half of its perimeter. For three rectangles the net gain is $\frac12\times20=10$ cm, so the new perimeter is $30+10=40$ cm.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Run Ze writes down all the integers with the following properties: the first digit is 1; each of the following digits is at least as large as the digit before it; the sum of the digits of the integer is 5. How many integers does he write?

solutions.title: List them
solutions.body:
The digits after the 1 sum to 4 and are non-decreasing (and at least 1): 11111, 1112, 113, 14, 122. That is 5 integers.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: What is the largest number of shapes of this form (an L-shaped piece of four unit squares) that can be cut out from the $5\times5$ square shown on the right?

solutions.title: Upper bound and construction
solutions.body:
Each shape covers 4 squares and the grid has 25, so at most $\lfloor25/4\rfloor=6$ shapes fit. It is possible to cut out 6 shapes (leaving one square), so the answer is 6.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Luigi opened a small restaurant. His friend Giacomo gave him some square tables and some chairs. When he tried to arrange all the tables as single tables with four chairs each, he found he had six chairs too few. When he decided to arrange the tables in pairs with six chairs for each pair of tables, he found he had four chairs left over. How many tables did Luigi receive from Giacomo?

solutions.title: Set up equations
solutions.body: Let there be $2x$ tables. Chairs: $4\cdot2x-6=8x-6$, and also $6x+4$. So $8x-6=6x+4$, $x=5$ and there are 10 tables.

solutions.title: Compare the two plans
solutions.body:
Per pair of tables, plan 1 needs 8 chairs and plan 2 uses 6. The difference per pair is 2 chairs, and the total difference is $6+4=10$ chairs. So there are $10\div2=5$ pairs, i.e. 10 tables.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Lily wants to make a large triangle from small triangular tiles. She has already put some tiles together, as shown in the diagram. What is the smallest number of small tiles that she now needs to complete a large triangle?

solutions.title: Smallest enclosing triangle
solutions.body:
The shape contains a line of five tiles with further tiles on each side, so the large triangle has a side with at least seven tiles. A triangle with 7 tiles along its longest row has $7+5+3+1=16$ tiles, and it can be built around the given shape (which has 7 tiles). So $16-7=9$ more tiles are needed.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Three vertices of the rectangle $PQRS$ are at $P(1,1)$, $Q(7,4)$ and $R(5,8)$. What are the co-ordinates of $S$?

solutions.title: Translate a side
solutions.body: $PQ$ and $SR$ are parallel and equal. From $P$ to $Q$ is $+6$ in $x$ and $+3$ in $y$, so $S=R-(6,3)=(-1,5)$.

solutions.title: Use the centre
solutions.body:
The diagonals bisect each other. The midpoint of $QS$ equals that of $PR$, which is $(3,4.5)$. So $S=2(3,4.5)-(7,4)=(-1,5)$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: A large cube was built from eight equally-sized small cubes, some of which were painted black and some painted white. Five of the faces of the large cube are shown in the diagram. What does the sixth face of the large cube look like?

solutions.title: Count black squares
solutions.body:
Each small cube shows three of its faces on three faces of the large cube, so the total number of black squares over the six faces is a multiple of three. The five faces shown have $2+1+1+1+1=6$, so the sixth face has 0 or 3 black squares, leaving options A and E. In E two black squares would share an edge, but no shown face has two such squares adjacent. So the sixth face is all white.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: A rectangular swimming pool of length 20 m is surrounded on all four sides by a path 2 m wide. The area of the path is the same as the area of the pool. What is the width, in metres, of the pool?

solutions.title: Total area is double
solutions.body:
Let the width be $Y$. The pool plus path is $24\times(Y+4)$ and equals twice the pool area: $24(Y+4)=40Y$, so $96=16Y$ and $Y=6$.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Kirsten wrote numbers in five of the ten circles arranged around a pentagon, as shown in the diagram. She wants to write a number in each of the remaining five circles so that the sums of the three numbers along each side of the pentagon are equal. Which number should she write in the circle marked $X$?

solutions.title: Compare adjacent sides
solutions.body:
Call $p$ the empty corner circle on the left, $q$ the empty corner circle at the bottom left and $r$ the empty corner circle at the bottom right. The side through $3$ and $7$ has corners $p$ and $7$, and the next side has $p,1,q$. Equal sums give $7+3+p=p+1+q$, so $q=9$. The side $q,6,r$ and the side $r,2,X$ give $q+6+r=r+2+X$, so $X=q+4=13$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Joey is playing with his calculator. He starts with the number 12 and then multiplies or divides by 2 or by 3 until he has done 60 calculations. Which of the following could not be his answer?

solutions.title: Parity argument
solutions.body:
Each calculation changes the exponent of 2 or of 3 in the result by exactly 1, so after 60 calculations the total change in the two exponents is even. Now $12=2^2\cdot3$ and $36=2^2\cdot3^2$ differ by 1 in total, which is odd, so 36 is impossible. The others differ from 12 by an even total: $18=2\cdot3^2$ (change $-1+1$), $72=2^3\cdot3^2$ ($+1+1$), $108=2^2\cdot3^3$ ($+2$), $12$ (change 0). Each can be reached by using some of the calculations in cancelling pairs such as $\times2$ then $\div2$.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: The digits of the three-digit integer $XYZ$ are all different. The sum of the digits of the three-digit integer $XXY$ is the two-digit integer $YZ$. The sum of the digits of the two-digit integer $YZ$ is the one-digit integer $Y$. What digit does $X$ represent?

solutions.title: Translate to equations
solutions.body:
$Y+Z=Y$ gives $Z=0$. Then $2X+Y=10Y$, so $2X=9Y$. Hence $2X$ is a multiple of 9, so $X=9$ and $Y=2$.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: Two three-digit integers have all six of their digits distinct. The first digit of the second integer is twice the last digit of the first integer. What is the smallest possible sum of two such integers?

solutions.title: Minimise the hundreds digits
solutions.body:
The hundreds digits sum to at least 5: either $1$ and $4$ (last digit 2 in the first number) or $2$ and $3$ (with a last digit 1). In the first case the tens digits can be 0 and 3; in the second 0 and 4, so the first case is better. Example: $102+435=537$.

**Answer: (C)**
